rules.statement: In a Backend-for-Frontend, never return an access, refresh or ID token to the browser in any endpoint response, header or cookie; the browser gets only an HttpOnly session cookie.
rules.why: Injected script has the same privileges as the application, so any token the browser can reach can be stolen and used from anywhere (RFC 10017 §5).
rules.check: Look for BFF endpoints, user/session documents, headers or cookies that serialize token values, and for token-mediating designs that hand the access token to the SPA.

rules.statement: Don't add options that disable a security control such as callback binding, cookie attributes, CSRF checks, the return-URL allow-list or the proxy allow-list; a setting may only select an equal or stronger behavior.
rules.why: The library is correct by default with no off switch, so misconfiguration cannot weaken it.
rules.check: Look for new boolean or enum options that turn off or relax a security check (e.g. `DisableCsrf`, `SameSite=Lax`/`None`, wildcard allow-lists).

rules.statement: Never put tokens, session handles, subjects or request paths in events, metrics, traces or logs.
rules.why: Telemetry must be observable without leaking credentials or user-identifying data.
rules.check: Inspect log messages, event payloads, metric tags and activity tags for token values, cookie/session handles, `sub` values or request paths.

rules.statement: Model an extensible vocabulary (token requirements, client-authentication methods, frontends, gates, claim shaping and similar) as registered strategies, not as a closed enum or switch statement.
rules.why: Vocabularies are open unless provably closed, so hosts can add entries without modifying the library.
rules.check: Look for new enums or `switch` statements over a kind/method name where new values would require editing library code instead of registering a strategy.

rules.statement: Make service contracts public interfaces with internal `Default*` implementations, and make options classes sealed with an accompanying validator.
rules.why: These are the family's conventions for library packages.
rules.check: Look for public implementation classes of service interfaces, implementations not named `Default*`, unsealed options classes, or options without a validator.

rules.statement: Keep BFF login transactions and sessions as server-side records keyed by random values rather than state protected by an ASP.NET Core Data Protection key ring.
rules.why: Without a Data Protection key ring there is no shared key ring to distribute and rotate across replicas.
rules.check: Look for `IDataProtector`/`AddDataProtection` or encrypted cookie/state payloads used for login state or session data in BFF code.

rules.statement: Make a BFF session cookie an opaque 256-bit random handle, store the session under a hash of the handle, and encrypt its tokens with a key derived from the handle.
rules.why: A dump of the session store alone then yields no usable token.
rules.check: Look for session stores keyed by the raw handle, tokens stored in plaintext, handles shorter than 256 bits, or cookies carrying session data rather than an opaque handle.

rules.statement: Accept a BFF session cookie on API calls only behind the layered CSRF defense: a required static custom header, cross-origin calls denied by default, Fetch Metadata checks, and `SameSite=Strict` cookies.
rules.why: Cookie-authenticated APIs are exposed to CSRF, and RFC 10017 §6.1.3.3 describes this layered defense.
rules.check: Look for API endpoints authenticated by the BFF cookie that skip the anti-forgery header or Fetch Metadata check, allow cross-origin by default, or set a weaker SameSite.

rules.statement: When a BFF forwards a call to a remote API, forward only to explicitly allow-listed destinations, normalize the path, strip inbound credentials such as cookies and Authorization, and never follow redirects.
rules.why: RFC 10017 §6.1.3.6 requires this so the forwarder cannot be turned into an open proxy or leak credentials.
rules.check: Look for forwarding that builds destinations from request input, skips path normalization, copies inbound Cookie/Authorization headers, or enables automatic redirect following.

rules.statement: Refresh a session's tokens single-flight across the whole cluster, so only one replica at a time redeems a given refresh token.
rules.why: A rotated refresh token presented twice trips reuse detection, and the OP then revokes the whole token family.
rules.check: Look for refresh code that only uses an in-process lock or no coordination at all, letting concurrent requests or replicas redeem the same refresh token.

rules.statement: Make a BFF OAuth client a confidential client that authenticates with `private_key_jwt` or mTLS and uses authorization code with PKCE `S256`, uses PAR when the OP advertises it, checks the RFC 9207 `iss` response parameter, and binds tokens with DPoP when the OP supports it.
rules.why: This is current best practice for a server-side OAuth client.
rules.check: Look for client secrets in place of assertions, missing PKCE or `plain` PKCE, skipped `iss` validation, or code that ignores PAR/DPoP metadata the OP advertises.

rules.statement: Don't implement the implicit, hybrid or password flows or a token-mediating backend in a browser-facing client.
rules.why: These flows put tokens where script can reach them, and RFC 10017 does not recommend them.
rules.check: Look for `response_type` values containing `token`/`id_token`, password grant requests, or endpoints that return an access token to the SPA.

rules.statement: In a relying-party library, rely only on standard OP metadata and endpoints, with no adapter or special case for one identity provider.
rules.why: The library must work with any compliant OpenID Provider. The reference OP is a test oracle, not a dependency.
rules.check: Look for hard-coded endpoint paths, provider-specific branches, or references to OP server packages in client code.
